title: Antim ardas: for him, or for us?
hookLine: the bhog and final Ardas close the mourning
carry: the final prayer asks rest for them, strength for us
tomorrow: the mourning is officially over. why is Bebe still crying?

lines: FOR BABA'S SOUL, OR FOR US?
cards: The gurdwara hall is fuller than Simran expected: truckers in clean shirts, Gurnam flown in from far away, Maya and her mom near the back. The granthi reads the closing pages of the Granth.
That's the bhog, the completion. Then the whole sangat stands for the antim ardas, the final prayer. On the drive home, an aunty says, so beautiful, the ardas for Baba's soul.
Harjit, eyes on the road, says quietly, it's for us, really. Simran, in the back seat, can't tell which of them is right.

teach.b: Both views live inside the Sikh community, so let each speak. First, the aunty. The final prayer is for him.
In the Ardas, the sangat asks Waheguru to give the one who has gone a place at the Guru's feet. A community stands together and asks, out loud, on behalf of someone who can no longer ask for himself.
That's love with somewhere to go.

teach.h: ANG 472: DEEDS CAN'T BE SENT ON.
teach.b: Now Harjit. The final prayer is for us.

Guru Nanak, in Asa ki Vaar on Ang 472, mocks a custom of feeding others in the ancestors' name: in paraphrase, if a thief robs a house and gives the goods in his ancestors' name, the goods are recognized in the next world, and he makes his ancestors thieves.
What a person did travels with them; nobody can send it on afterward. So the prayer is for the living: strength to accept the Will, and to carry on well.
And here's the thing worth telling a friend tonight: in the Ardas Simran heard, both requests were there.
Rest at the Guru's feet for Baba. For the family, the strength to accept the Will. The aunty and Harjit each heard half of it.

how: When the reading begun after a death reaches its bhog, the sangat stands for the antim ardas, asking peace for the departed and strength for the family to accept the Will; karah prashad and langar follow.

o: the first prayer said for a newborn baby
a vow of silence kept for a set number of days
the standing prayer that closes the mourning

games.q: the last page — tap the pairs.

s: antim ardas means the final prayer
antim, final; ardas, the standing prayer of petition.
Guru Nanak taught that gifts given in the ancestors' name reach them
Ang 472: a thief's gift in his ancestors' name only makes them thieves.
the antim ardas only asks something for the one who died
the Ardas Simran heard asked rest for Baba and strength for the family.

games.q: your friend's family is planning the final prayer for her grandfather. her brother says it's pointless because 'he can't hear it.' what's the best case for the other side?
o: he's right; prayers after a death don't do anything.
it's a community asking out loud, on his behalf, for his rest.
it's tradition, so you just do it without asking why.
games.why: the aunty's view at its best: a community stands and asks for someone who can't ask for himself. and the same Ardas asks strength for the living.

practice: If you pray, stand or sit straight with your palms together, the way the sangat stands for Ardas, and hold in mind someone who has died.
If not, keep the posture and simply remember them: a face, a laugh, one thing they used to say.

wordCard.voice: Antim ardas: the final prayer, said standing when the complete reading reaches its bhog, closing the formal mourning.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: antim ardas, the final prayer at the close of the reading after a death.

carryVoice: Keep this: the final prayer asks rest for them, strength for us, in one breath. That's it for today.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 472 (Asa ki Vaar, Guru Nanak: the thief who gives in his ancestors' name), paraphrased
